A design/product argument against the PR's explicit premise rather than a defect; its concrete consequences are covered by the specific findings elsewhere. Boundary call — a maintainer could reasonably want this debate, hence low confidence.

Confirmed against the vendored Kysely: #ensureNoMissingMigrations runs unconditionally in getState and throws 'corrupted migrations: previously executed migration ... is missing', so deleting the already-applied migration file makes runMigrations throw at boot for any database that recorded it.

Verified via the schema this PR partially reverts: rating previously carried `.transform(v => v === 0 ? null : v)`, so 0 really did coerce to null before the restriction and now 400s; the partial revert leaves that behavior changed with no test pinning it.

The extraction side of the original restriction is unreverted — validateRange(exifTags.Rating, 1, 5) still nulls -1 — so an XMP-authored or written-back rejection is silently dropped on the next extraction, defeating the PR's stated purpose.

Same defect as the human thread on those exact spec lines: moving the bounds into .refine() drops them from the JSON-Schema emitter, so the published spec and generated clients now advertise minimum/maximum of the safe-integer limits instead of the real range.
A cleared probe concluding the .nullable().refine().optional() chain is equivalent to the old .nullish(); correct, and it asserts no defect.

Confirmed against the commit being partially reverted: the client-side changes (web Rating type, mobile rating bar / search filter models) are untouched here, so no first-party client can produce -1 even though the API accepts it again.

ExifResponseDto.rating still declares .min(1).max(5) and the emitted ExifResponseDto publishes minimum 1 / maximum 5, while exifInfo.rating can now be -1; no runtime break today because no handler uses ZodSerializerDto, but the response contract and generated clients are wrong.
